findings.evidence: The four `@[expose]` declarations occur at lines 100–101, 203–204, 291–293, and 364–366, with `weightedIntersection_apply`, `picToCoker_mk`, `degree_mk`, and `picCongr_mk` immediately supplying usable API.
findings.fix: Remove `@[expose]` from all four definitions and retain their existing application lemmas as the supported interface.
findings.issue: `weightedIntersection`, `picToCoker`, `degree`, and `Equiv.picCongr` are all `@[expose]` even though lines 105, 209, 300, and 370 provide characteristic application lemmas; consumers can therefore depend on quotient/matrix implementation details.

findings.evidence: The Equiv section at lines 365–383 contains only `picCongr_mk` and `degree_picCongr`; `rg` finds no `picCongr_refl`, `picCongr_trans`, or inverse lemma.
findings.fix: Add `@[simp]` laws for `refl.picCongr`, `(f.trans g).picCongr`, and `f.symm.picCongr`/the inverse of `f.picCongr`, proved via `picCongr_mk`.
findings.issue: `Equiv.picCongr` has only an action-on-representatives lemma, with no identity, composition, or inverse laws, so equality and reindexing chains require quotient induction and unfolding rather than functorial rewriting.

summary: The public surface unnecessarily exposes implementation bodies and leaves the Picard equivalence without its basic functorial laws.
